title: Why AI Agents Are Becoming Products, Not Just Features

From App Stores to Agent Marketplaces But an AI agent marketplace can’t simply be a directory This could also create an economy for AI creators The developer becomes a product creator But agents need standards I think the market will evolve in three stages Stage 1 — Build Stage 2 — Discover Stage 3 — Trust This is why I’ve started thinking about Tuvaxo The bigger shift The question I’m watching Nisarg Satasiya AI Artificial Intelligence Product Management Bussiness Why AI Agents Are Becoming Products, Not Just Features Nisarg Satasiya 8 min read · Oct 10, 2026 -- Listen Share Press enter or click to view image in full size For years, the software industry followed a familiar pattern. A company built software. Then it added features. Then competitors added similar features. Eventually, almost every major software product had the same checklist: AI assistant AI writing AI search AI recommendations AI automation AI became a feature. But something different is starting to happen. AI agents are becoming products in their own right. And I think this distinction will matter more than most people realize. AI started as a feature Think about how AI entered mainstream software. A CRM added AI-generated emails. A project management tool added an AI assistant. A design tool added image generation. A document application added summarization. A customer support platform added an AI chatbot. The pattern was simple: Existing product + AI feature And there is nothing wrong with that. For many use cases, it’s exactly what users need. But AI agents introduce another possibility. Instead of adding AI to an existing product, you can build an entire product around an agent whose primary purpose is to perform a job . That’s a very different proposition. A feature helps you do the work Imagine your CRM has an AI feature. You open a customer record. You click “Generate Follow-Up.” The AI writes the email. You review it. You send it. Useful. But the human is still driving the process. Now imagine something different. You tell an agent: “Follow up with qualified leads that haven’t responded in seven days.” The system finds the relevant leads. It checks their history. It determines whether they qualify. It prepares the appropriate message. It sends the follow-up. It updates the CRM. It schedules the next action. The difference isn’t simply that the second system has better AI. The difference is responsibility . The first system helps you perform the task. The second system is responsible for carrying out the workflow. This is the shift from features to products A feature usually answers: “How can we help the user do something?” An agent product increasingly asks: “What can we do on the user’s behalf?” That’s a much bigger question. And it changes how software can be designed. Instead of starting with: Dashboard → Buttons → Features → User actions You can start with: Goal → Agent → Tools → Actions → Outcome The interface becomes secondary. The outcome becomes primary. Consider a sales agent Let’s take sales as an example. A traditional sales software product might give you: Lead database Email templates CRM Analytics Sequences Tasks Reminders The salesperson operates all of it. Now imagine an AI sales agent. Its job is: Find and qualify potential customers. It might: Identify potential companies. Research them. Find relevant decision-makers. Evaluate fit. Personalize outreach. Send messages. Monitor responses. Update the CRM. Escalate qualified opportunities. The product isn’t really the dashboard. The product is the work being performed. That’s the fundamental change. AI agents could create a new type of software business This is where things get interesting for founders. Traditional SaaS usually sells access to software. You might pay: $20 per user per month. Or: $100 per seat per month. The value is tied to the software being used. But an AI agent could potentially be priced around: Tasks completed Conversations handled Leads qualified Documents processed Hours of work Transactions Outcomes That creates a different economic model. Instead of: “Pay us to use our software.” The proposition becomes: “Pay us to perform this work.” That’s a very different relationship between software and customer. The rise of the digital specialist Another reason I think agents will become products is specialization. Humans specialize. You don’t hire one employee to be equally good at sales, accounting, legal research, customer support, software engineering and graphic design. You hire specialists. AI agents are likely to follow a similar path. Instead of one giant “AI assistant,” we could have specialized agents for: Sales Find and qualify leads. Customer Support Handle customer questions. Recruiting Source and screen candidates. Research Gather and analyze information. Finance Monitor transactions and prepare reports. Marketing Research markets and generate campaigns. Operations Monitor workflows and identify problems. Development Build, test and maintain software. Each agent has a specific job. That makes them much easier to understand and evaluate. But this creates a new problem Imagine the number of AI agents increases dramatically. Today, finding software is already difficult. Search for: “CRM” and you’ll find thousands of options.
